transcript.text: my belling cooker keeps burnin stuff 1 day then next day its undercookd on same temp. been like it a cuple months. thermastat??

Yes — a faulty thermostat/temperature sensor is a common cause, but it could also be the oven element, fan, door seal, or electronic control.

If it burns food one day and undercooks it the next at the same setting, the oven is probably not holding a steady temperature. After a couple of months it’s worth getting it checked rather than just compensating with the dial.

Things you can try first:

• Use an oven thermometer placed in the centre of the oven. Preheat for 20–30 minutes and see whether it stays near the set temperature or swings wildly.
• Check it is fully preheating — some ovens’ indicator lights go off before the whole cavity is properly hot.
• Look at the heating element (electric oven): bulges, splits, sparking, or only part of it glowing can mean it is failing.
• Check the fan (fan oven): it should run smoothly; a failed/intermittent fan causes hot and cold areas.
• Check the door seal for gaps, tears or flattening, and make sure the door closes properly.
• Try a different shelf position, but major day-to-day variation is not normal.

Avoid using it unattended or for anything safety-critical until it is fixed, especially if it is overheating. If you notice burning smells, smoke, tripping electrics, sparks, or a gas smell, switch it off/isolate it and arrange repair urgently.

A cooker engineer can test and replace the thermostat/sensor or control board. If you give me the Belling model number and say whether it’s gas, electric, fan, or conventional, I can narrow down the most likely fault.

its electric, a fan one, double oven. belling 60cm but i cant find the model number, label must be hidden behind the drawer thing. i dont have a thermometer either. the knob is a bit wobbly tho, and i dont always preheat fully, sometimes i just pop the lasagne straight in

Not fully preheating will definitely make a difference, especially with a cold lasagne — the stated cooking time/temperature normally assumes the oven is already at temperature. Put it straight in from cold and it can take noticeably longer.

But it shouldn’t be burning things one day and leaving them undercooked the next if you are using the same oven/function and roughly the same routine. The wobbly knob is worth taking seriously too.

Possible causes, roughly in order:

• Knob is loose/worn or not turning the thermostat spindle properly. The number it points to may not be the temperature it is actually selecting.
• Thermostat/temperature sensor/control fault — oven overshoots or fails to reach temperature.
• Fan not running consistently or heating element starting to fail. A fan oven can still get warm but cook very unevenly/slowly if one part fails.
• Using different cavities or settings accidentally. On a double oven, make sure you are comparing the same oven and the same fan setting each time.

What to do now:

1. For a few cooks, always preheat properly. Set it to, say, 180°C fan, wait until the heat light goes out, then give it another 10 minutes. Use the middle shelf.
2. Check the fan: with the main oven switched on to fan cooking, you should hear it and usually feel air movement when you carefully open the door briefly. If it is silent, intermittent, scraping, or weak, stop relying on that oven and get it repaired.
3. Check the loose knob: don’t force it or try to recalibrate anything. If it pulls off easily, switch the cooker off at the wall isolator first, then you can see whether the plastic inside the knob is cracked/rounded. A loose knob alone may be a cheap replacement; a loose spindle behind it needs an engineer.
4. Buy an inexpensive oven thermometer if possible — they are usually around £5–£10. It is the quickest way to prove whether “180” is actually 150, 220, or fluctuating.
5. Until it is sorted, use a food thermometer for things like chicken/mince dishes if you have one: the centre should be at least 75°C. Don’t rely purely on the timer when the oven is behaving unpredictably.

For the model number, check:
• around the oven door frame when the door is open;
• the side/rear of the cooker;
• inside/behind the bottom storage drawer (often on a rating plate);
• paperwork, old delivery emails, or the retailer order.

If you pull the drawer out, don’t dismantle panels or touch wiring. Many drawers pull fully open then lift slightly to come off the runners, but it varies by model.

Given it has been happening for months, I’d arrange a cooker engineer rather than keep compensating with the knob. Tell them: “Belling 60 cm electric fan double oven, inconsistent temperatures, possible loose thermostat knob.”
